title: Episode 58: The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald: The November Gale of Lake Superior
description:
The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald: The November Gale of Lake Superior. How a 729-foot iron ore freighter and her twenty-nine-man crew vanished into the icy depths of Lake Superior on November 10, 1975, during a hurricane-force blizzard. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the maritime mystery immortalized in American ballad and memory.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. On November 10, 1975, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald, a massive seven-hundred-and-twenty-nine-foot iron ore freighter and the proud Queen of the Lakes, was fighting for survival on Lake Superior. Battling hurricane-force winds of eighty miles per hour and monstrous thirty-foot waves in the freezing dark of a ferocious November gale, her veteran captain Ernest McSorley radioed a trailing vessel with six simple words: 'We are holding our own.' Minutes later, the massive ship vanished from radar screens without sending a distress call, taking all twenty-nine crew members into the freezing depths. George brings us the haunting true story of the Edmund Fitzgerald.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: QUEEN OF THE GREAT LAKES
When she was launched on the Detroit River in June nineteen fifty-eight, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald was the largest ship ever to sail the Great Lakes, earning the proud title Queen of the Lakes. Measuring seven hundred and twenty-nine feet long and seventy-five feet wide, with a cavernous hold capable of carrying twenty-six thousand long tons of iron ore pellets, she was an engineering marvel and a commercial workhorse of American heavy industry. For seventeen years, the Fitzgerald set cargo records, hauling millions of tons of concentrated taconite ore from the northern mines of Minnesota down through the Soo Locks to the blast furnaces of Detroit, Cleveland, and Gary, Indiana. To lake sailors, she was known affectionately as The Big Fitz or The Pride of the American Side, celebrated for her speed, luxury crew quarters, and handsome blue-and-white livery. The massive freighter was the pride of Oglebay Norton Columbia Transportation Division, equipped with modern navigation gear, dual radar units, and wood-paneled officers quarters that made her the envy of the lakes. In early November nineteen seventy-five, the ship was under the command of Captain Ernest M. McSorley, a sixty-three-year-old master mariner with forty-four years of Great Lakes experience who was planning to retire after the season. McSorley knew Lake Superior temper better than any man alive, but even he could not anticipate the lethal meteorological trap closing around his ship. The crew of the Fitzgerald was a tight-knit brotherhood of experienced lake sailors from Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, men who had spent their working lives navigating the vast inland seas. Captain McSorley was widely regarded as one of the steadiest, most capable captains on the lakes, known for his meticulous adherence to safety and calm leadership during hazardous weather.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: LOADING AT SUPERIOR AND THE APPROACHING LOW
On Sunday afternoon, November ninth, nineteen seventy-five, the Edmund Fitzgerald was tied to the Burlington Northern ore dock in Superior, Wisconsin, taking on twenty-six thousand one hundred and sixteen tons of taconite pellets. At two fifteen that afternoon, under crisp gray autumn skies, Captain McSorley gave the order to cast off lines and began steaming eastward across Lake Superior toward Detroit. Shortly after departure, the Fitzgerald was joined by the SS Arthur M. Anderson, another large ore carrier commanded by Captain Jesse Bernie Cooper, which lagged ten to fifteen miles behind. The National Weather Service had issued a standard gale warning predicting strong southerly winds, but within hours, two separate low-pressure systems merged over the Great Lakes, intensifying into a monstrous cyclone. By early morning on Monday, November tenth, the storm was designated a full winter hurricane, with barometric pressure plummeting to twenty-nine inches and wind gusts exceeding seventy-five knots. Recognizing the rising peril, Captain McSorley and Captain Cooper altered course northward, seeking the protective lee of the Canadian shoreline along the northern rim of Lake Superior to shield their heavily laden vessels from towering open-water waves. As the twin freighters steamed into northern waters, barometric readings plunged at an alarming rate of one millibar per hour, signaling the approach of a once-in-a-decade maritime monster. The storm sucked freezing Canadian polar air southward across the open waters of Lake Superior, creating steep, unpredictable seas that battered the hulls with bone-rattling force from the beam.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE WHITE HURRICANE UNLEASHED
By Monday afternoon, November tenth, the storm pivoted viciously to the northwest, sweeping directly over open water and stripping away the shelter of the Canadian shore. The Fitzgerald was caught in the worst possible maritime vortex: a freezing white hurricane of blinding horizontal snow, freezing spray, and sustained gale-force winds of sixty knots with gusts surpassing eighty miles per hour. Waves on Lake Superior rose to thirty and thirty-five feet—immense walls of black, freezing water with vertical faces that slammed into the Fitzgerald steel superstructure with hundreds of tons of concussive force. At three fifteen in the afternoon, Captain McSorley radioed Captain Cooper on the trailing Anderson to report serious structural damage: Anderson, this is the Fitzgerald. I have a bad list, I have lost both of my radar antennas, and I have lost two vent covers and taken on some water. My pumps are running, but I will slow down so you can close the gap. McSorley was effectively blind in zero-visibility blizzard conditions, navigating without radar through treacherous shoal waters off Caribou Island, relying entirely on radio guidance from the Anderson. Without functioning radar, McSorley was forced to rely on dead reckoning and intermittent radio checks with Captain Cooper on the Anderson. Heavy spray froze upon the pilothouse windows, blinding the watchstanders as snow flurries reduced forward visibility to barely a few boat lengths, leaving the captain to navigate solely by compass and instinct amidst towering waves.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SHOALS OF CARIBOU ISLAND
To this day, maritime historians and naval architects debate whether the Fitzgerald touched bottom as she passed Six Fathom Shoal, a treacherous underwater reef north of Caribou Island. The Six Fathom Shoal was marked on Canadian navigational charts as shallower than previously reported, and in monstrous seas that generated immense wave troughs of twenty to thirty feet, a heavily loaded ship with a twenty-seven-foot draft could easily scrape bottom. Crew members aboard the Anderson watched the Fitzgerald radar pip pass suspiciously close to the shoal. If the vessel struck the granite reef, the impact would have cracked keel plates, ruptured ballast tanks, and breached the cargo hold beneath thousands of tons of dense taconite ore. Taking on water along her bottom plates would explain why the vessel developed a pronounced starboard list and began sitting sluggishly low in the water, unable to rise readily over oncoming crests. Meanwhile, onshore, hurricane winds had severed power lines to the Whitefish Point Lighthouse and its radio beacon, depriving McSorley of his last visual and electronic landfall reference. Great Lakes sailors have long warned of the treacherous shoals surrounding Caribou Island, where sudden underwater pinnacles rise within fathoms of the surface. In the violent wave troughs of that ferocious gale, an eight-hundred-foot ship pitching in heavy seas could easily slam onto the jagged rock, causing catastrophic bottom damage that would remain hidden beneath thousands of tons of cargo.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE THREE SISTERS AND THE FINAL CALL
Shortly after seven o clock on Monday evening, the storm unleashed its ultimate fury upon the trailing Anderson. A legendary Great Lakes phenomenon known as The Three Sisters struck the vessel: three successive, rogue monster waves, each thirty to thirty-five feet high, slammed into the Anderson stern in rapid succession. The massive waves buried the Anderson deck beneath twelve feet of solid green water, drove her bow down, and carried away lifeboats before rolling forward toward the Fitzgerald. Captain Cooper later testified that the rogue waves swept directly down the track where the Fitzgerald was struggling fifteen miles ahead. At seven ten in the evening, Anderson first mate Morgan Clark radioed the Fitzgerald: Fitzgerald, how are you making out with your problems? Captain McSorley answered in a calm, steady voice: We are holding our own. It was the final transmission ever received from the Edmund Fitzgerald. Less than fifteen minutes later, at seven twenty-five, Clark looked at the Anderson radar screen: the Fitzgerald radar target had vanished completely into the clutter of the storm. Repeated radio calls met only the hiss of static. The Three Sisters were legendary among Great Lakes mariners as the most terrifying phenomenon of open-water gales: three massive, closely spaced rogue waves that could overwhelm a vessel before it could clear water from its deck. If the battered Fitzgerald encountered these monstrous walls of water while already sluggish, she would have had no opportunity to recover.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SEARCH IN THE GALE
When Captain Cooper could not raise the Fitzgerald on any radio frequency, he contacted the United States Coast Guard station in Sault Ste. Marie to report the ship missing. But the Coast Guard had no vessels capable of surviving the hurricane-force seas on open Lake Superior. In an act of supreme courage, Coast Guard controllers asked Captain Cooper and the crew of the Arthur M. Anderson to turn their ship around in the raging thirty-five-foot seas and return to the Fitzgerald last known position to search for survivors. Cooper bravely agreed, joined hours later by the SS William Clay Ford. For two days, search vessels and Coast Guard aircraft scanned the freezing waters near Whitefish Bay. They found only empty, shattered lifeboats, life preservers, and oil slicks floating on the icy chop. Not a single one of the twenty-nine men aboard had survived, nor was a single body ever recovered from the frigid depths of Lake Superior. The heroic response of Captain Cooper and the crew of the Arthur M. Anderson exemplified the highest traditions of maritime service, turning their ship back into hurricane-force waves to search for their lost comrades. Despite harrowing danger to their own vessel, they searched through the blizzard until dawn, driven by the desperate hope of finding survivors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BELL OF THE MARINERS CHURCH
In May nineteen seventy-six, a U.S. Navy submersible equipped with underwater cameras located the shattered wreckage of the Edmund Fitzgerald lying in Canadian waters, five hundred and thirty feet beneath the surface of Lake Superior, just seventeen miles from the safety of Whitefish Bay. The massive steel hull had broken cleanly in two upon hitting the lakebed, buried deep in soft clay. The official Coast Guard marine casualty report concluded that the ship likely took on water through faulty hatch covers, causing her bow to nose-dive into a giant wave and plunge straight to the bottom without warning. In nineteen ninety-five, at the request of the victims families, the ship bronze bell was respectfully raised from the wreckage and replaced with a replica bearing the engraved names of all twenty-nine crewmen. Immortalized in Gordon Lightfoot haunting nineteen seventy-six folk ballad, the Edmund Fitzgerald remains the ultimate symbol of the perils of Great Lakes shipping. Every November tenth, the historic Mariners Church in Detroit rings its bell twenty-nine times for the men of the Edmund Fitzgerald, ensuring that the crew who braved the November gale will never be forgotten. The tragic loss of the Edmund Fitzgerald led to sweeping safety reforms in Great Lakes shipping, including mandatory survival suits, automated distress beacons, and improved hatch inspections for all bulk freighters. The twenty-nine men of the Fitzgerald are forever remembered as symbols of the brave souls who harvest the riches of the northern waters.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Edmund Fitzgerald sleeps beneath the icy waves of Lake Superior, an enduring testament to the power of the inland seas. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we investigate the tragic and forgotten Bath School disaster of 1927.
